title: What is a Prometheus rule? - A Comprehensive Guide
summary: A Prometheus rule runs a PromQL expression on a schedule. Learn how to configure recording rules, alerting rules, and notifications.
body_markdown:
# What is a Prometheus rule? - A Comprehensive Guide


Last Updated: October 27, 2026


11 min read


A Prometheus rule tells the[Prometheus monitoring system](https://signoz.io/guides/what-is-prometheus-for-monitoring/) to evaluate a PromQL expression at regular intervals. These rules help you put frequently used calculations and alert conditions into your monitoring configuration, so you don't have to run the same queries by hand.


There are two types of rules. Recording rules save the results of a query as new time series, which can reduce repeated query work on dashboards. Alerting rules detect conditions that need attention and trigger alerts when those conditions are met. Together, they help you keep dashboards responsive and find problems without watching them constantly.


This guide covers how to configure and test both types of rules, how Prometheus alerts move through their lifecycle, and how to connect Prometheus to Alertmanager for notifications. It also covers ways to reduce alert noise and manage rules over time.


## Understanding recording rules in Prometheus


Recording rules in Prometheus are designed to precompute frequently used or resource-intensive queries. They save the results as new time series, so you can query those results instead of repeatedly running the original complex query.


For example, create a file named` rules.yml


`


with this recording rule to calculate the request rate for each service:


```text
groups  :
-   name  :   service_requests
rules  :
-   record  :   service:http_requests:rate5m
expr  :   sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
```


In this example,` rate()


`


calculates the average per-second increase in` http_requests_total


`


over five minutes for each input series.` sum by (service)


`


adds those rates across instances and other labels, leaving one result per service.


The recording rule saves that result as` service:http_requests:rate5m


`


. You can query this metric instead of repeating the full expression. If your metrics use different names or labels, update the expression accordingly.


The name` service:http_requests:rate5m


`


follows the` level:metric:operations


`


convention:` service


`


is the grouping level,` http_requests


`


identifies the source metric, and` rate5m


`


describes the calculation.


## Alerting rules in Prometheus


An alerting rule defines a condition that Prometheus checks at regular intervals. When the condition is met, Prometheus creates an alert for each matching time series. If the condition remains active for the configured duration, the alert fires.


An alerting rule can include the following fields:


```text
-   alert  :   <alert_name>
expr  :   <PromQL_expression>
for  :   <duration>
labels  :
<label_key>  :   <label_value>
annotations  :
<annotation_key>  :   <annotation_value>
```


### Example: Alert on high CPU usage


Add the following` cpu_alerts


`


group to` rules.yml


`


, below the` service_requests


`


group from the recording rule example. The rule alerts when an instance's average CPU usage stays above 90% for five minutes:


```text
-   name  :   cpu_alerts
rules  :
-   alert  :   HighCPUUsage
expr  :   100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100) > 90
for  :   5m
labels  :
severity  :   critical
annotations  :
summary  :   "High CPU usage detected on {{ $labels.instance }}"
description  :   "CPU usage has been above 90% for five minutes on {{ $labels.instance }}."
```


The expression calculates the five-minute rate of idle CPU time, averages it across CPU cores for each instance, and subtracts that percentage from 100. The result represents non-idle CPU usage. If it remains above 90% across evaluations for five minutes, the alert fires for that instance. This example uses` node_cpu_seconds_total


`


, a metric exposed by[Node Exporter](https://signoz.io/guides/prometheus-node-exporter-metrics/) .


Prometheus sends firing alerts to configured Alertmanager instances. Alertmanager can then group and route notifications. An alert can fire without a notification being sent immediately.


### Use label matching to select services


You can use a regular expression in a label selector to check more than one job. For example, this expression finds failed scrapes for targets in either job:


```text
up{job=~"important-service|critical-app"} == 0
```


A failed scrape tells you that Prometheus could not collect metrics from a[target](https://signoz.io/guides/what-is-prometheus-target/) , but it does not reveal the cause. A target that disappears from service discovery may no longer have an` up


`


series, so this expression does not detect every missing target.


### Combine alert conditions


You can combine conditions when an alert should fire only if both are true. For example, the following expression selects services with a 5xx error rate above 5% and a 90th-percentile request duration above one second:


```text
(
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
> 0.05
)
and on (service)
max by (service) (http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.9"}) > 1
```


The error-rate calculation uses` http_requests_total


`


with` service


`


and` status


`


labels. The duration expression uses a summary metric with a` service


`


label, that takes the highest reported 90th percentile among instances, rather than calculating a service-wide percentile.` and on (service)


`


matches these two conditions by service.


Before using the expression in your own setup, check the metric names and labels and make adjustments accordingly. To quickly become familiar with PromQL query syntax, check out our[PromQL cheat sheet](https://signoz.io/guides/promql-cheat-sheet/) .


Use a` for


`


duration to avoid firing on brief spikes. For example, changing the CPU rule to` for: 15m


`


requires the condition to remain active for 15 minutes. Alertmanager can also group related alerts to reduce notification noise.


## Load, validate, and reload your rules


To make Prometheus evaluate the recording and alerting rules, add` rules.yml


`


to the` rule_files


`


list in` prometheus.yml


`


:


```text
global  :
evaluation_interval  :   30s


rule_files  :
-   rules.yml
```


In this example,` evaluation_interval: 30s


`


tells Prometheus to evaluate rules every 30 seconds. If you don't set it, the default is one minute. An individual rule group can set its own` interval


`


; rule evaluation and scraping run on separate schedules.


Before loading the rules, check both files with` promtool


`


:


```text
promtool   check   rules   rules.yml
promtool   check   config   prometheus.yml
```


Run these commands with paths to your files. The checks can catch syntax and configuration errors, but they cannot tell you whether the metrics exist or whether your alert threshold is appropriate.


Next, reload the configuration by sending` SIGHUP


`


to the Prometheus process. If Prometheus was started with` --web.enable-lifecycle


`


, you can instead send a reload request:


```text
curl   -fsS   -X   POST   http://localhost:9090/-/reload
```


Use your Prometheus address and authentication settings if they differ from the example. After the reload, open` http://localhost:9090/rules


`


and check that the` service_requests


`


and` cpu_alerts


`


groups are loaded without evaluation errors. Query` service:http_requests:rate5m


`


to inspect the recording rule's output. You can also check` http://localhost:9090/alerts


`


for pending or firing` HighCPUUsage


`


alerts.


## Connect Prometheus to Alertmanager


Prometheus evaluates alerting rules, but it needs Alertmanager to route notifications. To send a notification when the` HighCPUUsage


`


alert fires, configure Prometheus to send alerts to Alertmanager, then configure Alertmanager with a notification receiver.


If Alertmanager is not installed, get it from the[Prometheus downloads page](https://prometheus.io/download/) . Add its address to your existing` prometheus.yml


`


configuration:


```text
alerting  :
alertmanagers  :
-   static_configs  :
-   targets  : [  'localhost:9093'  ]
```


In this example,` localhost:9093


`


points to an Alertmanager running on the same host as Prometheus. If they run in separate containers or on different machines, use an address that Prometheus can reach. Check and reload the Prometheus configuration after adding the address, as described in the previous section.


## Configure a notification receiver


Alertmanager needs a route to decide where to send alerts and a receiver to deliver the notifications. For example, create an` alertmanager.yml


`


file with a webhook receiver:


```text
route  :
receiver  :   platform-webhook
group_by  : [  'alertname'  ,   'job'  ]
group_wait  :   30s
group_interval  :   5m
repeat_interval  :   4h


receivers  :
-   name  :   platform-webhook
webhook_configs  :
-   url  :   'https://alerts.example.com/prometheus'
send_resolved  :   true
```


The route sends alerts to` platform-webhook


`


and groups them by alert name and job. It waits 30 seconds before sending the first notification for a new group. Later notification updates are checked every five minutes, and unchanged firing alerts can be repeated after four hours. With` send_resolved: true


`


, the receiver can also send notifications when alerts resolve.


Replace the example URL with an endpoint that accepts Alertmanager's webhook payload. For Slack, email, or PagerDuty, use the corresponding receiver configuration instead. Check the configuration, then start Alertmanager with it:


```text
amtool   check-config   alertmanager.yml
alertmanager   --config.file=alertmanager.yml
```


If Alertmanager is already running, reload its configuration with` SIGHUP


`


or an HTTP POST to its` /-/reload


`


endpoint. Open the Alertmanager UI, usually on port 9093, to check that firing alerts arrive. Then test delivery with a controlled alert and confirm that the receiver gets the notification. An alert appearing in the UI alone does not confirm delivery.


## How the Prometheus alert lifecycle works


Prometheus tracks each alert by its labels and evaluates its state at regular intervals. For the` HighCPUUsage


`


rule, each instance moves through these states:


State What it means


Inactive The instance does not match the alert expression.


Pending CPU usage is above 90%, but the condition has not remained active for five minutes.


Firing CPU usage has remained above 90% across evaluations for five minutes.


If the condition clears while the alert is pending, the alert returns to inactive. Without a` for


`


duration, an alert can fire on the first matching evaluation. A firing alert becomes inactive when it stops matching, unless` keep_firing_for


`


extends it. Alertmanager may then send a resolved notification, depending on the receiver configuration.


Once an alert fires, notification timing depends on Alertmanager as well. For example, if` HighCPUUsage


`


becomes pending at 12:00 and stays active through each 30-second evaluation, it can fire at 12:05. With` group_wait: 30s


`


for a new alert group, Alertmanager can send the first notification around 12:05:30, plus delivery time. If the alert resolves before` group_wait


`


ends, no initial notification is sent for it.


For an existing group,` group_interval


`


controls when Alertmanager checks for changes, and` repeat_interval


`


controls when an unchanged firing alert is eligible for another notification. In the configuration above, those values are five minutes and four hours. Scrape timing, routing, and delivery can also affect when a notification arrives.


## Reduce alert noise and flapping


An alert can repeatedly fire and resolve when a metric moves back and forth across a threshold. This is called flapping. The` for: 5m


`


setting in the CPU rule helps by waiting for high CPU usage to persist before firing.


You can also add` keep_firing_for


`


to the` HighCPUUsage


`


rule, alongside` for


`


:


```text
for  :   5m
keep_firing_for  :   2m
```


With this setting, the alert keeps firing for two minutes after the condition was last met. This can prevent repeated resolutions during brief recoveries or gaps in data, but it also delays resolution.


Alertmanager provides other ways to manage notifications.` Grouping


`


combines related alerts into a notification, while` Silences


`


temporarily mute alerts that match selected labels.` Inhibition


`


suppresses matching notifications while another alert is active, such as an alert for a dependency failure.` Silences


`


and` Inhibition


`


do not stop Prometheus from evaluating rules.


Choose delays based on how quickly your team needs to respond. Review noisy alerts before increasing thresholds or wait times, and include enough context in annotations for the recipient to investigate.


## Test and troubleshoot Prometheus rules


Use` promtool test rules tests.yml


`


to test rules against synthetic input series and expected results. Include the pending period, threshold boundaries, and recovery in your tests.


Problem What to check


Rule missing from the Rules page Check` rule_files


`


, file paths, permissions, and reload errors.


Recording rule returns no data Run its expression directly and check metric names, label selectors, and recent samples.


Alert stays pending Check whether it has remained active for the full` for


`


duration and whether changing labels keep creating new alert instances.


Alert does not fire Check the expression's returned series, missing data, thresholds, and evaluation errors.


Alert fires but no notification arrives Check the Prometheus-to-Alertmanager connection, matching routes, receiver errors, grouping delays, silences, and inhibition.


Rule evaluations are slow or fail Inspect the expression's cost, cardinality, query timeout, and Prometheus resources. Reuse recording rules where they avoid repeated work.


Monitor` prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total


`


for evaluation failures. Increasing the evaluation interval reduces how often rules run; it does not itself increase the query execution timeout.


## FAQs


### Can I use PromQL functions in rules?


Yes, you can use any valid PromQL expression in both recording and alerting rules, including functions.


### Does a pending alert send a notification?


Prometheus does not send pending alerts to Alertmanager for notification. The alert must fire first. Alertmanager can then apply routing, grouping delays, silences, and inhibition before delivering a notification.


### Do I need Alertmanager for recording rules?


No. Prometheus evaluates and stores recording rule results itself. Alertmanager handles alert notifications, not recording rule evaluation.
